doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Jazz education and New York jam sessions
title: Jazz moving into academia: information without innovation
summary: Players learn from books and school, with little room to find their own sound; she urges them to move the audience, and Rowe agrees older players learned on the street.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: It’s like it’s very bizarre but I can’t remember who I was speaking with, maybe somebody at IAJE but some other musicians, and they were saying the place of the jazz

artist is really going into academia now, and into the colleges. And you can tell by the way the students play. It’s so interesting that it’s — I won’t say cookie cutter — because all the kids, certain ones have different talents, but there’s so much information about how to learn. So much information and so little innovation, you know, in what the new artists, the young artists, are doing. It’s either duplicating styles or attitudes or whatever you call it, artists that came before them, or else it’s everybody trying to play like John Coltrane. And you can really easily because a lot of what he did or Charlie Parker, a lot of the drummers or pianists, it’s all in a book. You can open a book and go oh here’s track number seven from the “Milestones” album. Okay, let me see how — and they learn stuff that way. So everything is getting so high and proficient with like harmony and technique, and everybody has all this information and knows all this and that and there’s nowhere to go with it except in school. There’s no jobs and nobody has the opportunity to play all the time and create their own like uniqueness. It’s all in the context of the school. And I find that odd. Because it takes a really long time to get players to loosen up and open up, and when they’re playing, like in my big band I see it all the time, which has a lot of young women in it. And you don’t have to play all those things that you learned in school, all those phenomenal licks and all those chord substitutions. Nobody cares. Why you’re going to make a living playing jazz is if you make somebody’s heart go thumpeta thumpeta, thump. And you sit there and I’m always trying to say what moves you guys? And I was talking about it last night with Anat, one of our tenor players. And she’s brilliant. And she’s got all the chops and technique in the universe, but just to get her to go like honk be de det, and like play something and the audience is like yaaay, if she plays something interesting that’s not like [scats] look how fast I can play, nobody cares.
I’m so pleased to hear you say that actually.
Oh good. I mean I don’t care either.

Because as you say, jazz has become academic and there are so many different ways to explain what people did and then you can just absorb it and do it I guess. And of course time goes by and things change, but when you talk to the older veterans, they learned on the street and they learned in the jam session. They didn’t seem to need all that instruction.
